summary: Describes the goals and requirements for network mobility, which arises when a router moves with an entire network and its point of attachment to the Internet changes. The aim is to keep sessions between nodes in the mobile network and the wider Internet working during the move. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4886 describes what network mobility support should achieve when a router moves a connected network. Its requirements aim to keep devices reachable and their sessions working without requiring changes to those devices.

questions: what are the goals of network mobility
how does nemo basic support work
subtitle: Goals and requirements for keeping a network reachable as its router moves

tldr.problem: When a router moves a whole network to a new Internet connection, the network's location changes and active sessions can break.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4886 states design goals and requirements for NEMO Basic Support, including reachability through a bidirectional tunnel between a mobile router and its Home Agent.
tldr.outcome: The document records requirements for the basic solution and identifies route optimization as separate future work. It is Informational, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 4886 is an Informational goals-and-requirements document published in July 2007. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: When an Entire Network Moves
sections.content:
A mobile network moves when its connecting router changes its point of attachment to the Internet. Devices behind that router may stay physically where they are, but their location in the Internet's routing structure changes.

Without network mobility support, those devices can lose Internet access and ongoing sessions can break. RFC 4886 states the goals for keeping them reachable as the mobile router moves.
sections.plainLanguage: A mobile router connects a group of devices to the Internet. When that router moves, the devices should remain reachable and keep their sessions.

sections.title: Design Goals for Network Mobility
sections.content:
The design goals include keeping permanent addresses usable, limiting packet loss and delay during handovers, and requiring mobility support only in the mobile router. The mechanism should work at the IP layer so applications and other upper-layer protocols can continue unchanged.

The RFC also calls for support for varied network layouts, backward compatibility with IPv6 standards, secure signaling, location privacy, IPv4 and network-address-translation traversal, and limited impact on global Internet routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The router should handle the move without changing the devices or their applications. The solution should also limit disruption, protect signaling, and avoid burdening Internet routing.

sections.title: Basic Support and the Home Agent Tunnel
sections.content:
The NEMO working group chose a stepwise approach: first define basic support for session continuity, then study more efficient routing for nested or complex networks. RFC 4886 says the basic solution reuses Mobile IPv6 methods.

For basic support, each mobile router has a Home Agent and maintains a bidirectional tunnel to it. The mobile router obtains a Care-of Address at its current attachment point, while nodes in the mobile network remain reachable through their permanent addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic support sends traffic between the moving router and a Home Agent through a tunnel. Devices inside the network keep their permanent addresses.

sections.title: Requirements and Further Work
sections.content:
The basic-support requirements say that all traffic between a mobile network node and an Internet correspondent must pass through the router-to-Home-Agent tunnel. The solution must support at least two levels of nested mobile networks, and it must protect signaling so the receiver can authenticate and authorize the sender and detect replay.

RFC 4886 says route optimization and other extended-support issues were being studied, but the working group was not then chartered to standardize an extended-support solution. The RFC itself describes goals and requirements rather than defining the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic design sends network traffic through the tunnel and secures its control messages. More direct routing for nested networks is outside this document's requirements.
